pos: n. (the second month of the sacred year, in which Solomon began the temple)
etymology: Hebrew Ziv, brightness, or splendour, the month of blossom; the pre-exilic name of the second month, later called Iyyar; named twice, 1 Kings 6:1 and 6:37.
biblical_def: Zif is the old Hebrew name of the second month, and Scripture uses it only to date the beginning of the temple: “And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month Zif, which is the second month, that he began to build the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 6:1). The notice is repeated when the account turns to the building's measurements: “In the fourth year was the foundation of the house of the LORD laid, in the month Zif” (1 Kings 6:37). The completion is dated by the same reckoning in another old month name: “And in the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, was the house finished throughout all the parts thereof, and according to all the fashion of it. So was he seven years in building it” (1 Kings 6:38). The sacred year began at the exodus by divine appointment, and its first month kept the older name too: “This day came ye out in the month Abib” (Exodus 13:4). Zif means brightness, the month when the land is in blossom, and the house of the LORD was begun in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Zif, brightness, or the month of blossom; the second month of the Hebrew sacred year, in which Solomon began to build the temple; afterward called Iyyar.

corruption_summary: Biblical chronology is treated as vague or symbolic; the building of the temple is dated to a named month of a named regnal year, four hundred and eighty years after the exodus.
corruption_paragraphs: A commonplace of modern treatment is that Scripture has no real interest in chronology and that its numbers are theological rather than historical. 1 Kings 6 is a hard case for that claim. It gives the month, the regnal year, the interval since the exodus, the duration of the work, and the month of completion — the kind of dating an ancient building inscription gives, and the kind a later theological construction has no reason to invent in such detail.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's works are done in time and that Scripture dates them. The sacred calendar itself was reordered at the exodus, so that Israel counted its year from redemption; the temple was begun in the month of blossom and finished seven years later in the month of rain. Our faith rests on events with dates, which is why the creeds name a Roman governor.

pos: n. (the ninth month of the Hebrew year)
etymology: Hebrew Kislev, of uncertain derivation, possibly from a root meaning hope or confidence; the ninth month, answering to parts of November and December; named twice, Nehemiah 1:1 and Zechariah 7:1.
biblical_def: Chisleu is the ninth month of the Hebrew year, and both of its appearances in Scripture mark a moment of grief or inquiry. The first opens Nehemiah's book: “The words of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah. And it came to pass in the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace” (Nehemiah 1:1), and what he did on hearing of Jerusalem's ruin follows at once: “And it came to pass, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 1:4). The second is a dated prophecy: “And it came to pass in the fourth year of king Darius, that the word of the LORD came unto Zechariah in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu” (Zechariah 7:1), and the word that came was a question about the people's fasting: “Speak unto all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?” (Zechariah 7:5). In one Chisleu a man fasted rightly; in another the LORD asked a nation whether its fasting had been for Him at all.

corruption_summary: Fasting is practised as a technique for results or dismissed as legalism; Zechariah has God ask whether the nation's seventy years of fasts had been directed to Him at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Fasting is handled badly in two directions. Some treat it as leverage on God, a discipline that obliges Him to act; others treat it as an obsolete work and drop it. Zechariah 7 cuts between them with a question that is still the sharpest thing said on the subject: the people had fasted in the fifth and seventh months for seventy years, and the LORD asked, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me? The practice had become about itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the contrast Scripture sets up within the same month. Nehemiah heard bad news, sat down, wept, fasted and prayed before the God of heaven, and then spent the rest of his life acting on what he had prayed. That is fasting directed to God and issuing in obedience, and it is the pattern the prophet's question is meant to produce.

pos: n. (the tenth month of the Hebrew year, in which Esther was taken to the king)
etymology: Hebrew Tebeth, probably from a root meaning to sink or to be muddy, the month of winter rain; the tenth month, answering to parts of December and January; named once, Esther 2:16.
biblical_def: Tebeth is named once in all of Scripture, and it dates the hinge of the book of Esther: “So Esther was taken unto king Ahasuerus into his house royal in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign” (Esther 2:16). What came of it is the next verse: “And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti” (Esther 2:17). Years later Mordecai would tell her what the crown had been for: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). The book of Esther never once names God, and it is the most pointed demonstration of providence in the canon. A Jewish orphan is taken into a pagan harem in the month of winter rain, and a nation is preserved by it.

corruption_summary: Esther is read either as a feminist heroine acting on her own initiative or as a compromised participant in a pagan court; the book presents her as an instrument of a providence it never names.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposed modern readings both miss the book. One makes Esther a self-authored heroine whose courage is the point; the other condemns her for complicity in Ahasuerus's harem and treats the story as a cautionary tale. The text does neither. It reports her situation without excusing the court, has Mordecai locate the deliverance in God's purpose rather than in her bravery — deliverance arise to the Jews from another place — and then shows her risking her life in obedience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence without a visible hand. God is not named in Esther, no miracle occurs, no prophet speaks, and yet every coincidence runs one way: a sleepless night, a forgotten chronicle, a gallows built for the wrong man. A date in the month Tebeth sits at the start of it. The believer who sees no sign of God in his own circumstances is reading the book he is in.

pos: n. (the eleventh month of the Hebrew year, in which Zechariah received his night visions)
etymology: Hebrew Shebat, of uncertain derivation, possibly from a root meaning to smite or to beat, the month of late winter; the eleventh month, answering to parts of January and February; named once, Zechariah 1:7.
biblical_def: Sebat is named once, and it dates the night of Zechariah's visions: “Upon the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Sebat, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying” (Zechariah 1:7). The call that had come a few verses before is the summons the whole book turns on: “Therefore say thou unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 1:3). What the visions of that night promised is given plainly: “Therefore thus saith the LORD; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem” (Zechariah 1:16). The dating matters because the people were discouraged: the temple foundation had lain exposed for years and the returned remnant had stopped building. In the month of late winter, with nothing yet to show, a prophet was given eight visions of a city measured for rebuilding and a Branch who would build it.

corruption_summary: Prophetic vision is treated as timeless religious imagery; Zechariah's visions are dated to a day, a month and a regnal year, and addressed to a specific building project that had stalled.
corruption_paragraphs: Apocalyptic literature is the part of Scripture most readily detached from history and read as symbol floating free of circumstance. Zechariah refuses the treatment. His visions are dated to the twenty-fourth day of Sebat in the second year of Darius, given to a named man with a named father and grandfather, and aimed at a discouraged remnant that had quit work on the temple. The horses, the measuring line, the candlestick and the flying roll all speak into that.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God speaks into the stalled and ordinary situation, and that His word runs past it. The same visions that got the temple rebuilt also show the Branch, the stone with seven eyes, the priest crowned as king, and the one they pierced. Dated prophecy is not small prophecy. It is prophecy you can locate, and therefore prophecy you can test.

pos: n. (the youngest son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab and Abishai, one of David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew Asahel, God hath made, or made of God, from asah, to make or do, and El, God; borne by several men, chiefly David's nephew, 2 Samuel 2:18.
biblical_def: Asahel was the youngest of David's three warrior nephews, and Scripture introduces him by the gift that killed him: “And there were three sons of Zeruiah there, Joab, and Abishai, and Asahel: and Asahel was as light of foot as a wild roe” (2 Samuel 2:18). At the pool of Gibeon he outran Abner and would not be waved off; Abner warned him three times and then struck: “Howbeit he refused to turn aside: wherefore Abner with the hinder end of the spear smote him under the fifth rib, that the spear came out behind him; and he fell down there, and died in the same place: and it came to pass, that as many as came to the place where Asahel fell down and died stood still” (2 Samuel 2:23). The death set a blood feud running that cost Abner his life under a flag of truce: “And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother” (2 Samuel 3:27). He is nevertheless numbered with the best men in Israel: “Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (2 Samuel 23:24). Several later Levites bear the name; this Asahel is the one the narrative follows.

corruption_summary: Courage is celebrated as its own virtue; Asahel's refusal to turn aside was courage without judgment, and it cost him his life and Abner his.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that prizes boldness as an unqualified good has nothing to say about Asahel except that he was brave. The narrative is more careful. He was the fastest man in the army and he used it to run down the most dangerous soldier in Israel alone; Abner, who did not want the blood of Joab's brother on him, told him three times to take another man's armour instead and turn aside. He refused to turn aside, and the text pauses on the men who stopped where he fell. Valour without counsel is how young men die.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the long reach of blood vengeance, and why God took it out of private hands. Asahel's death gave Joab a grievance he nursed until he could murder Abner in a city gate under a truce, which David cursed and which Solomon finally avenged. The law's cities of refuge and its requirement of witnesses and judges exist precisely because a brother's blood, left to a brother, never stops.

pos: n. (the second son of Benjamin, head of the family of the Ashbelites)
etymology: Hebrew Ashbel, of uncertain derivation, rendered a man in God, or reproof of God; named three times, Genesis 46:21, Numbers 26:38, 1 Chronicles 8:1.
biblical_def: Ashbel is named in all three of the Benjamite registers. He appears in the company that went down into Egypt: “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21). He heads a counted family in the wilderness: “The sons of Benjamin after their families: of Bela, the family of the Belaites: of Ashbel, the family of the Ashbelites: of Ahiram, the family of the Ahiramites” (Numbers 26:38), and the census closes “These are the sons of Benjamin after their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and six hundred” (Numbers 26:41). Centuries later the Chronicler gives him his birth order: “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1). Three lists, taken centuries apart, agree that Benjamin had a son called Ashbel and that his house endured. The tribe was nearly destroyed in the days of the judges and rebuilt from six hundred men; that his family name survives all three registers is the kind of detail Chronicles was written to preserve.

corruption_summary: Agreement across registers taken centuries apart is treated as literary harmonising; the plainer account is a family name kept through Egypt, the wilderness, and a near-extinction.
corruption_paragraphs: The three Benjamite lists are a favourite exhibit for source criticism, since they differ in several names and in order. What is less often noticed is where they agree. Ashbel is in all three, in the same relative position, with a family named after him in the census and a birth order given in Chronicles. A tradition being invented late does not produce that sort of partial, awkward agreement; it produces tidiness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the preservation of a house through judgment. Between the census of Numbers and the register of Chronicles lies the atrocity at Gibeah, after which Benjamin numbered six hundred men. The Ashbelites are counted at full strength on one side of that and the family name still stands on the other. God kept a tribe that deserved to be erased, and from it gave Israel Saul, Mordecai and Paul.

pos: n. (the title of the Roman emperor; of Caesar Augustus at the birth of Christ, and of Nero in Paul's appeal)
etymology: Latin Augustus, venerable, majestic, consecrated, from augere, to increase; a title granted to Octavian in 27 BC and borne by his successors; named four times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Augustus is in Scripture twice over: once as the emperor whose census brought Joseph to Bethlehem, and once as the title of the emperor to whom Paul appealed. The first is the opening of the nativity: “And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed” (Luke 2:1), and the effect of that decree is the next thing recorded: “And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:)” (Luke 2:4). The second is Festus reporting Paul's appeal: “But when Paul had appealed to be reserved unto the hearing of Augustus, I commanded him to be kept till I might send him to Caesar” (Acts 25:21) — where the emperor is Nero. The title also attaches to a military unit: “And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band” (Acts 27:1). The word means venerable, and the Latin of the day used it of what was consecrated to the gods.

corruption_summary: Imperial power is treated as the engine of history; Scripture has the greatest emperor of the age issue a tax decree whose whole function in the narrative is to move a carpenter to Bethlehem.
corruption_paragraphs: The emperor who called himself Augustus, the venerable, and whom the empire worshipped as the son of a god and the bringer of peace, appears in Luke's Gospel for exactly one sentence, and that sentence exists to explain why a pregnant woman was on the road to a village in Judaea. The evangelist is not overawed. He uses the census the way a writer uses weather. Rome's own propaganda hailed Augustus as saviour and the inaugurator of a golden age; Luke dates the real Saviour's birth by his paperwork.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the empires. A prophecy spoken seven hundred years earlier required the Christ to be born in Bethlehem, and the mechanism God used was the tax administration of a pagan emperor who had never heard of Micah. Paul later appealed to that same office and was carried to Rome at imperial expense to preach there. Kings are tools in this story, and they do not know it.

pos: n. (one of Solomon's twelve officers, over the country of Gilead)
etymology: Hebrew Geber, a man, or a strong man, from gabar, to be strong or to prevail; named once as a personal name, 1 Kings 4:19.
biblical_def: Geber held the largest and most exposed of Solomon's twelve districts: “Geber the son of Uri was in the country of Gilead, in the country of Sihon king of the Amorites, and of Og king of Bashan; and he was the only officer which was in the land” (1 Kings 4:19). The system he served in is described at the head of the list: “And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision” (1 Kings 4:7). A few verses earlier the Authorized Version names a Ben-geber over Ramoth-gilead, and the margin reads that name as the son of Geber, so the family may have held the east bank in two commissions. The land he administered had been taken from Sihon and Og in the days of Moses, and the description of the kingdom he fed is one of the high-water marks of Israel's history: “Judah and Israel were many, as the sand which is by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking, and making merry” (1 Kings 4:20). His name means simply a man, or a mighty man, and he was the only officer in a province that had been two kingdoms.

corruption_summary: Administration is thought unspiritual beside prophecy and worship; Scripture names the twelve men who fed Solomon's kingdom and the months they served.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a persistent piety that counts only the prophetic and the devotional as spiritual, which leaves the long administrative passages of Kings and Chronicles looking like dead weight. The text disagrees by the space it gives them. Twelve officers, named, each responsible for a month's provision for the court, with their districts specified — and one man, Geber, carrying a province that had been two Amorite kingdoms, alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of competent government under God, and its limits. The chapter that names Geber ends with Israel dwelling safely, every man under his vine and fig tree; the same administrative machinery, extended by Solomon into forced labour and heavy taxation, is what split the kingdom under his son. Good order is a mercy and never a saviour, and Scripture shows both ends of it.

pos: n. (a head of a family of Manasseh, Gideon's clan; also the name of one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Abiezer, father of help, or my father is help, from ab, father, and ezer, help; named seven times, chiefly of the Manassite clan, Joshua 17:2.
biblical_def: Abiezer is one of the six Manassite families that received the inheritance west of Jordan: “There was also a lot for the rest of the children of Manasseh by their families; for the children of Abiezer, and for the children of Helek, and for the children of Asriel, and for the children of Shechem, and for the children of Hepher, and for the children of Shemida: these were the male children of Manasseh the son of Joseph by their families” (Joshua 17:2). The clan is best known as Gideon's: it was the first body of men to answer his trumpet, “But the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered after him” (Judges 6:34), and Gideon himself used its name to turn away a quarrel: “And he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?” (Judges 8:2). The Chronicler traces the family's origin through a woman: “And his sister Hammoleketh bare Ishod, and Abiezer, and Mahalah” (1 Chronicles 7:18). A second and quite distinct Abiezer, the Anethothite, was one of David's thirty and captain for the ninth month.

corruption_summary: Gideon is remembered for the fleece and the three hundred; the text roots him in a named clan that answered first and then had to be talked out of a tribal quarrel.
corruption_paragraphs: Gideon is usually abstracted from his family and read as an individual case study in weak faith made strong. Judges keeps him in a clan. The Abiezrites were the men who gathered at his first trumpet, the altar he tore down was his father's, and the quarrel he had to defuse was between his clan's vintage and Ephraim's gleaning. His later failures — the ephod, the seventy sons, Abimelech — are clan failures too.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the name: my father is help. Gideon's clan was called Father-of-help, and Gideon's first recorded word is a complaint that the LORD had forsaken Israel. The deliverance came anyway, by three hundred men with pitchers, so that Israel could not say its own hand had saved it. Help belongs to God, and He arranges the circumstances so that nobody can mistake the source.

pos: n. (a son of Gilead, father of Zelophehad, head of the family of the Hepherites)
etymology: Hebrew Chepher, a well, or a digging, from chaphar, to dig or search out; named chiefly of the Manassite, Numbers 26:32.
biblical_def: Hepher heads one of the six Manassite families, and his house produced the most consequential legal case in the Pentateuch. He is counted in the wilderness: “And of Shemida, the family of the Shemidaites: and of Hepher, the family of the Hepherites” (Numbers 26:32), and the very next verse records the problem: “And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters: and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah” (Numbers 26:33). Those five women brought their claim to Moses: “Then came the daughters of Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, of the families of Manasseh the son of Joseph: and these are the names of his daughters; Mahlah, Noah, and Hoglah, and Milcah, and Tirzah” (Numbers 27:1), and the LORD ruled for them, establishing in Israel that a daughter inherits where there is no son. The ruling is applied at the division of the land: “But Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, had no sons, but daughters” (Joshua 17:3). Hepher the man is to be distinguished from the town of Hepher in Solomon's districts, and from Hepher the Mecherathite among David's men.

corruption_summary: Biblical inheritance law is cited as proof that daughters counted for nothing; the case of Hepher's granddaughters is the law establishing that they inherit when there is no son.
corruption_paragraphs: The claim that Scripture simply excluded women from property runs into Numbers 27 and cannot get past it. Five sisters of Hepher's house came to Moses, Eleazar, the princes and the whole congregation and argued that their father's name should not be done away for want of a son. Moses brought the cause before the LORD, and the LORD said the daughters of Zelophehad spoke right and commanded that the inheritance pass to them. It became a standing statute in Israel.

The complementarian reading has no difficulty here and never did. Scripture distinguishes offices from standing: eldership in the church and headship in the home are given to men, while property, legal standing, testimony and the covenant promises belong to men and women alike. The daughters of Zelophehad were granted land and a judgment in their favour, and when the ruling was later refined so that they married within their own tribe, it was to keep the inheritance in the family that had been given it. Hepher is remembered because his line ran out of sons and God made a law for it.
